standard.title: Objects, features and suitability
standard.description: make, compare and classify objects, identifying key features and explaining why these features make them suited to their uses
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can recognise, compare and classify shapes referencing the number of sides and using spatial terms such as opposite, parallel, curved and straight (AC9M2SP01). They have not yet connected shape features to purpose/use, or made and compared 3D objects with feature identification.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students make, compare and classify geometric objects, identifying key features and explaining why those features suit the object's purpose.

nodes.label: Identifying key features of objects
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify and name the key geometric features (faces, edges, vertices, curves) of common 3D objects.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify and count faces, edges and vertices for two 3D objects (e.g. cube, triangular prism); describe one key feature of each.
nodes.typical_width: Compare and classify a range of 3D objects by their geometric features; use formal language (prism, pyramid, cylinder, cone, sphere); describe similarities and differences.
wider: Investigate geometric features in natural objects — crystals, shells, seeds — connecting geometry to natural structures
Explore how First Nations Australians use geometric patterns and three-dimensional forms in art, architecture and tools
success_criteria: Students can identify and correctly count faces, edges and vertices of a given 3D object.
Students can classify objects using geometric feature language (faces, edges, vertices).

nodes.label: Features and suitability for purpose
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how the geometric features of an object make it suited to its everyday use.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain why the features of one common object (e.g. a cylinder can, a rectangular box) make it suited to its use.
nodes.typical_width: Compare several everyday objects and explain how their geometric features (shape, faces, stability, capacity) relate to their purpose; evaluate alternative designs.
wider: Design and make a 3D object for a specific purpose, explaining feature choices — connecting to Design Technologies
Investigate how architectural and engineering structures use specific geometric features for strength, stability or visual effect

response_modes.reason: Explaining suitability requires connecting geometry knowledge (node 1) with functional reasoning about the world. Students who can identify features but cannot explain their purpose haven't yet made the geometric-functional connection.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The design-and-make extension and architectural investigation provide strong cross-curricular richness connecting geometry to real-world function — genuinely extending understanding without acceleration.
success_criteria: Students can name at least one key feature of an object and explain how that feature suits its purpose.
Students can compare two objects and explain why one is better suited to a given use based on its geometric features.
